rv.q: This one, in particular, is an empathy machine that moved me greatly by its end.
What playwright Eboni Booth lacks here in scope and complexity, she makes up for with the quality of the work's warmhearted sentiment.

The smallness of PRIMARY TRUST is unique and touching. It’s really just a play about Kenneth’s identity journey and the small discoveries and friendships he forges along the way. And luckily director Malkia Stampley’s terrific ensemble in this Goodman production brings out all the emotional depth.
I'll even dare to say it's my favorite piece of theatre this year.
Do not miss this quiet, almost unassuming one-act play that's laced with warmth and good humor.
This winsome, touching, Pulitzer Prize-winning play turns so many theatrical conventions upside down that the surprise twist comes nearly at the beginning.
With an outstanding cast and an inspired creative team, the production offers a quiet yet profound reflection on human connection, personal growth, courage, and the essential need for primary trust.
But the night belongs to Steppenwolf Theatre Company ensemble Namir Smallwood and his masterful role as Kenneth.
Goodman Theatre's quietly riveting Chicago-area premiere stars Namir Smallwood — an actor of incandescent vulnerability and keen self-awareness...
Booth's play is expertly cast and directed by Malkia Stampley in what marks her impressive Goodman directing debut.
Smallwood is remarkable as Kenneth... his choices utterly believable and emotionally resonant without ever treading into overwrought territory.

What we learn about Kenneth and his best friend Bert is powerful. I don't like giving away important facts that might alter the play's affect on you, so I will tell you that their relationship is one where Bert entered Kenneth's life at a time of great despair and need.
